newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Merger seen fortifying Amplats for future.
newsitem.headline: Merger seen fortifying Amplats for future.

text.p: Merging mining companies will fortify South Africa's Anglo American Platinum Corp Ltd and enable it to optimise a united cash base and shared ore reserves, analysts said on Wednesday.
It was this future strength that made it possible for the world's largest platinum producer to plan for a big new mine and expand existing operations, they said.

"It is a good thing. It makes sense. It allows for the optimisation of all three ore reserves and they are substantial ore reserves. The optimal use of the cash also makes sense," said BOE Natwest platinum analyst Paul Brogan.
"Lebowa's debt would have been a hindrance to any expansion. Now they're going ahead with this expansion. It gives Amplats the flexibility it needs," Brogan added.

Amplats said yesterday it would merge into the parent company its three listed mining companies -- Rustenburg Platinum Holdings Ltd (Rusplat), Lebowa Platinum Mines Ltd (Leplat) and Potgietersrust Platinums Ltd (PP Rust).
It also said it would develop a new 1.2 billion rand mine at Boschkoppie and expand PP Rust's concentrator.
Boschkoppie would be developed as a division of Rusplat and would see about 250,000 ounces of newly-mined platinum being produced with full production reached in 2002.
The expansion at Boschkoppie and PP Rust would see Amplats increase production from around 1.8 million ounces of platinum a year to 2.1 million ounces.
Analysts said that the "sharing" aspect of the merger also meant that the mines would share costs, thereby reducing the overall unit cost for Amplats platinum production.

"As a company (the deal) makes it stronger because it brings it down the cost curve. It has a single cash flow to extend to each of the companies," said George Topping, mining analyst at Irish and Menell Rosenberg Inc.
But on Wednesday shares in the Amplats' companies did not perform well although there was much interest with more than 210,000 shares changing hands on an otherwise quiet day.
Rusplat lost 225 cents to 69 rand, PP Rust shed 70 cents to 25.50 rand, Lebowa was steady at 290 cents and Amplats itself cut 35 cents off its price to 28.50 rand.

Dealers and analysts said that the shares' weakness probably had more to do with the platinum price which was slipping in tandem with the sickly bullion price than with anxiety that the merger ratios might not favour current share prices.
Platinum was last bid at $364 an ounce, while gold was at $340.80 an ounce.
Analysts said there was no need for the market to worry about the new mine's production pressuring the metal's price with increased supply.

"Some think the expansion of production will delay any recovery in the platinum price but the expansion will take a while and by then the Russian stockpiles should have diminished and so I think we will still see a recovery," Brogan said.

"Amplats is actually being quite responsible in preparing for that deficit in the platinum market that lies ahead. They're planning to only bring on supply when the Russians are no longer selling from stockpiles," Topping said.
He added that there were some mines which would be unable to sustain production at current price levels and this too would remove some supply from the market.
